title: Research Bite #22: Cognitive Endurance as Human Capital
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #22 covers Brown et al.'s NBER working paper on cognitive endurance -- the ability to sustain effortful thinking without performance dropping off over time -- as a form of human capital in its own right. In a field experiment with Indian primary school students, the researchers randomly assigned children to sustained cognitive practice, either academic (math problems) or non-academic (games like mazes and tangrams), against a control group, and found both practice types measurably improved cognitive endurance, cutting the rate of performance decline across later tests. The gains showed up not just on lab measures but in classroom attentiveness and school performance, and partially persisted even after a long break from the intervention. Complementary quasi-experimental evidence showed additional schooling improves cognitive endurance mainly in higher-quality schools -- specifically those assigning more independent practice time -- which points to sustained, focused effort as the active ingredient rather than schooling in general. The classroom implication is that teachers can deliberately build endurance through independent practice and effortful tasks, while being alert to the fact that disadvantaged students fatigue faster, which has direct consequences for how long tests and tasks should run. This is not primarily an ed-tech study -- the intervention is entirely non-digital (paper math problems and physical puzzle games) -- so it belongs with pedagogy and learning-science research rather than technology-in-schools coverage.
points: The central finding that cognitive endurance improved from both academic and non-academic effortful-thinking practice, suggesting the active ingredient is sustained effort itself, not subject content.

Disadvantaged students were shown to experience cognitive fatigue more quickly than their peers, meaning long, unbroken tests and tasks may systematically disadvantage them independent of content knowledge.

The finding that schooling's benefit to cognitive endurance concentrates in higher-quality schools that assign more independent practice time -- pointing to a specific, replicable classroom lever rather than a vague "better schools" effect.
The gains partially persisted after a long break, suggesting cognitive endurance functions as a durable skill rather than a short-lived warm-up effect.
